item.title: Xi highlights Sino-US youth ties before visit
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-22
Xi highlights Sino-US youth ties before visit In reply to American students, he voices hope they'll help boost bilateral bonds President Xi Jinping has expressed the hope, in a reply to American university students ahead of his three-day state visit to the United States starting on Wednesday, that young people in China and the US will advance bilateral friendship and cooperation. Nearly 100 students from 10 US universities, including Harvard, had written to Xi about their experiences during exchange programs in China and their willingness to contribute to bilateral friendship. Xi said he was pleased to learn that the students had enjoyed a memorable trip and was heartened by their appreciation of Chinese civilization, their hopes for friendly cooperation between the two countries, and their willingness to serve as envoys of friendship across the Pacific. Xi emphasized that young people in China and the US share the same planet and shoulder the responsibilities of their times. He expressed the hope that the students would work with their peers in both countries to carry forward, safeguard and advance bilateral friendship and cooperation, promote mutual understanding between the two peoples, and help ensure the steady and sustained development of China-US relations, contributing their youthful energy to building a better world. The reply came as China's Foreign Ministry confirmed on Monday that Xi will make his first state visit to the US in 11 years. During the visit, President Xi and US President Donald Trump will hold in-depth discussions on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development, Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said at a regular news briefing. Head-of-state diplomacy plays an irreplaceable role in providing strategic guidance for bilateral relations, Guo said, adding that reciprocal visits by the two presidents within six months represent a historic milestone. China is ready to work with the US to give greater substance to a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, and properly manage differences to benefit both peoples and promote world peace, stability and prosperity, he added. The visit follows Trump's state visit to China in May, when Xi and Trump agreed on a new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, providing strategic guidance for bilateral ties over the next three years and beyond. Since Trump took office in January 2025, the two leaders have held two face-to-face meetings and five phone calls, and have written many letters to each other. Sun Chenghao, an associate research fellow at Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy, said that tariff reductions and an extension of the trade truce were key areas to watch. Putting earlier trade understandings into practice could help consolidate stability in bilateral economic ties, he added. Closer engagement could also help China and the US address challenges facing the wider world, said Zhu Feng, dean of Nanjing University's School of International Studies, highlighting their shared responsibility to support global peace, stability and development. Zhu said a more stable China-US relationship could bolster confidence in the global economy. He also stressed the importance of dialogue on regional conflicts and other international challenges, in order to help manage tensions and reduce the risk of miscalculation. Both sides need to show mutual understanding and respect on issues involving core interests and sensitive concerns, Zhu said, stressing that managing differences does not mean avoiding them. People-to-people exchanges are another important part of the relationship. Xi has emphasized on a number of occasions that the hope of China-US relations lies in the people and that the future depends on young people. In San Francisco in November 2023, he announced an initiative to invite 50,000 young Americans to China for exchange and study programs over five years. The target has been met two-and-a-half years ahead of schedule. Moritz Kuhlmann, an affiliated researcher at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis, hailed the initiative as a way to deepen mutual understanding. "We start with small steps, very narrow, very concrete," he said, "and that can evolve into something bigger." zhaojia@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Lanterns' revival illuminates ancient craft
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-22
Lanterns around Mid-Autumn Festival are often associated with nights of bright displays, festive crowds and elaborate illuminated installations. But in Nanjing, East China's Jiangsu province, there is another way to experience them. For this year's Mid-Autumn Festival, which falls on Sept 25, a revived lantern market is bringing more than 60 vendors, handmade lanterns, food and performances into the city's old lanes, giving visitors more reason to linger beyond simply looking at the lights. At Xi'nanli, a historical and cultural quarter in the heart of the city, visitors can follow glowing rabbit and lotus lanterns through the lanes, stopping for local snacks, browsing small shops, watching artisans make lanterns or trying their hand at the craft themselves. By night, the lanterns glow against gray-tiled roofs and historical facades, turning an ordinary walk through the old neighborhood into part of the festival. The historical Daqiao Lantern Market in Xi'nanli is a centuries-old facility that was once an important hub for lantern manufacturing and sales before Nanjing's lantern trade gradually shifted toward the better-known Confucius Temple area. Revived in 2020, the market has since evolved into a combination of lantern stores and craft experiences, food outlets, performances and activities that lead visitors through the old city. Zheng Longwu hasn't missed a single edition in recent years. The market has satisfied his nostalgia for the days when he would go to the Confucius Temple to see and buy lanterns. "There are many traditional designs, including fish and dragon lanterns, just the way I remember," said Zheng, who has lived in the neighborhood for more than five decades. Today, Xi'nanli is much closer to his home, about a 15-minute walk away. He still comes with his family, sometimes bringing his grandchildren to see the lanterns and buy one or two small ones. During the Qing Dynasty (1644-1911), lantern viewing during the festival was one of Nanjing's most eagerly anticipated pastimes, drawing crowds into the streets. Gan Xi, a Qing scholar and author of Baixia Suoyan, a collection of notes on old Nanjing, wrote that the Daqiao Lantern Market has existed "for a long time", describing crowds gathering around brightly colored silk lanterns. The streets became a spectacle of their own. Temporary stalls decorated with lanterns lined the roads, musicians played inside and performers in theatrical costumes passed through on stilts and in land boats. Now, visitors can again experience the tradition in the neighborhood where the market once flourished. For Chen Weixin, a cultural and architectural researcher whose organization has been involved in the development of Xi'nanli since 2008, bringing the market back is a way to reconnect the historical neighborhood with its past. "The lantern market is a way of drawing people into the old city. Once they come here for the lanterns, they begin to discover the neighborhood itself," Chen said. Visitors can wander past historical residences, decades-old buildings and structures from different periods of modern Nanjing, while cafes, shops and cultural venues occupy the same streets. The aim, Chen said, is to create a "living scene", where residents and visitors share the neighborhood. Over the years, traditional lantern maker Lu Min has taught foreign visitors, including those from Germany and Spain, to make lanterns by hand. For visitors wondering which lantern to take home, Lu recommends the lotus lantern. The lotus has long carried a cultural meaning in China because it grows from muddy silt yet blooms pure and bright. As such, it expresses a wish for integrity and a clean, upright life, Lu said.

item.title: APEC firms riding drive of modernization
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-22
APEC firms riding drive of modernization Foreign companies expand presence, tapping growing demand, innovation With China offering new opportunities through its vast market and continued opening-up, foreign businesses are expanding their presence, tapping growing demand and innovation while using the country as a base to serve markets across Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies. Market watchers said China's modernization drive and economic transformation are giving Asia-Pacific firms greater access to its vast and evolving market, advanced manufacturing capabilities and growing innovation ecosystem, helping deepen regional trade, investment and supply chain ties. Zhang Yuyan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences in Beijing, said China's push for high-quality development is giving businesses across the region a greater role in China's transformation. Echoing such a sentiment, Tu Xinquan, dean of the China Institute for WTO Studies at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said deeper economic integration across the Asia-Pacific is also raising demand for more efficient and resilient cross-border supply chains, as companies seek faster and more reliable links between producers and consumers. Against this backdrop, German logistics services provider DHL put its Shenzhen, Guangdong province super gateway into operation at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in late July with an investment exceeding 1.2 billion yuan ($179 million), marking its single largest investment on the Chinese mainland. John Pearson, CEO of DHL Express, said China's role in the global economy has fundamentally changed, evolving from primarily a manufacturing base into an increasingly important hub for innovation and consumer demand. "For companies across the Asia-Pacific region, China's industrial upgrading, expanding consumer market and advances in areas such as artificial intelligence, new energy and high-end manufacturing are creating new opportunities to invest, innovate and strengthen their global supply chains," said Pearson. The trend extends to manufacturers. Japanese industrial conglomerate Panasonic Holdings Corp put a new electronic materials plant into operation in Suzhou, East China's Jiangsu province, in late June, following an investment of 600 million yuan. Haruhiko Kuwata, director of the electronic materials business division at Panasonic Industry Co Ltd, a business unit of Panasonic Holdings, said the new plant will serve as a key production base as the company ramps up capacity to meet growing demand for electronic materials used in advanced applications. Honeywell Technology is also strengthening its innovation presence in China. The United States-based industrial group opened a new innovation center in Shanghai on Sept 1. The facility brings together its latest technologies and solutions across 12 immersive industry scenarios covering energy, smart manufacturing and infrastructure. Foreign direct investment in China's high-tech industries rose 35.1 percent year-on-year to 200.26 billion yuan in the first eight months, accounting for 41.7 percent of the country's total FDI inflows, up 12.4 percentage points from a year earlier, said the Ministry of Commerce. Sam Fischer, CEO of Australian vintner Treasury Wine Estates, said the company will continue to deepen its focus on the Chinese market, with China playing an increasingly important role in its long-term strategy. The strategy is backed by strong sales of its core brands, particularly Penfolds, whose sales in the Chinese mainland market rose 34.7 percent year-on-year during TWE's 2026 fiscal year ended June 30. zhongnan@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: China looks beyond medals at Asian Games
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-22
China looks beyond medals at Asian Games Event to gauge progress of broader strategy to build nation into sports 'powerhouse' China has topped the medal table at the Asian Games on 11 consecutive occasions. While they are aiming for 12 in a row at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, the success of their campaign in Japan will not be judged solely by the final tally of gold medals. As the competition unfolds, the Games will test whether China can turn dominance in its traditional strongholds into a broader and more balanced sporting strength. That means building greater depth in athletics, swimming and aquatic sports, and seeking improvement in football, basketball and volleyball. China has sent 815 athletes as part of its 1,274-member delegation to compete in 38 sports and 369 events. The athletes have an average age of 24, and 548 of them — nearly two-thirds of the team — are making their Asian Games debuts, placing generational renewal at the heart of the campaign. The Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, which run from Sept 19 to Oct 4, will also offer a good indication of how the country's competitiveness in a broad range of sports is evolving in the run-up to the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. The framework for that assessment is the "633" strategy set out in the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) for sports development, released by the General Administration of Sport of China in July. Sports administrators' stated goal is to build the country into a sports powerhouse. The 633 plan places 12 sports into three categories. They are the six traditional strengths — diving, gymnastics, weightlifting, shooting, table tennis and badminton; three foundational sports — athletics, swimming and water sports; and the three major ball sports — football, basketball and volleyball. At a State Council Information Office news conference in Beijing on Sept 3, Gao Zhidan, minister of the General Administration of Sport of China, said the country would "promote the comprehensive and balanced development of competitive sports". This, he said, requires a strategic shift from "making breakthroughs in key areas" to "comprehensive development" centered on the 633 sports during the five-year period. The Aichi-Nagoya Games provide a snapshot of that transition, with different sports facing different questions — from maintaining established advantages and renewing talent to expanding the competitive base and rebuilding strength in the three major ball sports.

item.title: The gardens emperors called home
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-22
Editor's note: The 2026 Beijing Culture Forum is being held in the Chinese capital from Sept 22 to 23, under the theme "Cultural Heritage and Mutual Learning Among Civilizations". In this ancient city, rich in cultural treasures, conservators and researchers are working tirelessly to preserve its heritage. China Daily reporters spoke with them on the eve of the forum to learn about their work and the inspiration behind it. The Forbidden City was where Qing Dynasty (1644-1911) emperors ruled. But Beijing's western gardens were where they increasingly chose to live. Emperor Kangxi began living and working in the Changchun Garden. From 1687 to 1722, he spent about 107 days there every year on average and even died in the garden. His son, Emperor Yongzheng, went further, spending more than 210 days a year during the last decade of his reign in the Yuanmingyuan (also known as the Old Summer Palace). Later, Emperor Daoguang surpassed them both, spending an average of more than 260 days a year there for most of his reign. Their keen interest turned the gardens from leisure retreats into another political center of the Qing government, alongside the Forbidden City. Numerous legends took root there, giving the gardens a special place in Chinese history. They later became collectively known as the Three Hills and Five Gardens, referring to Xiangshan, Yuquan and Wanshou Mountains, and five royal gardens: Jingyi Garden, Jingming Garden, Changchun Garden, Yuanmingyuan and the Summer Palace (Qingyi Garden). Located on the northwestern outskirts of Beijing, the area is now part of Haidian district. Centuries passed. The gardens, once representing the pinnacle of imperial garden design, gradually fell into ruin, were destroyed in wars, or gave way to modern buildings. Yet their memories remain vivid. In recent years, these historical mountains and gardens have reemerged, bringing their unique history and culture to modern visitors. Zhu Qiang, a scholar specializing in studies of the Three Hills and Five Gardens at the Beijing University of Agriculture, says the area, an ensemble of gardens, temples, military camps, paddy fields and tombs, has deep cultural connotations. Many parts were built as early as the Liao (916-1125), Jin (1115-1234) and Yuan (1271-1368) dynasties, although the overall layout took shape during the reigns of Qing Emperor Qianlong and his son Jiaqing. "Many places within the area blend features of tourist attractions elsewhere," says Zhu. "It not only had Tibetan-style buildings and complexes resembling those in the lower reaches of the Yangtze River, but also drew inspiration from Indian and Burmese cultural elements, traditional Chinese myths and Renaissance influences from Europe. In this sense, it was a carrier of cultural communication." Activities within the area were varied. Emperor Qianlong, for example, would visit his mother in Changchun Garden, meet officials or have breakfast in the West Garden, enjoy tea and boating at Yuquan Mountain, and finally return by boat to the Summer Palace before continuing to Yuanmingyuan by horse or sedan chair, says Zhu. However, as the dynasty waned, the gardens also declined. In 1860, Anglo-French forces looted and burned many of them. Although the Summer Palace and Jingming Garden were partly restored in the late Qing period, their former glory gradually faded. Following the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949, the ancient compounds were gradually protected and restored individually. Among them, the best-preserved Summer Palace was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998. In 2012, a new idea emerged: the Three Hills and Five Gardens should be protected as a whole, given their close historical connections. The idea was incorporated into Beijing's general city plan for 2016 to 2035, released by the city authorities in 2017. It outlined a 68.5-square-kilometer protective area — larger than Beijing's old city area of 62.5 sq km. In 2020, the Haidian Three Hills and Five Gardens National Cultural Relics Protection and Utilization Demonstration Zone was designated as one of China's first national-level demonstration zones of its kind, marking a new phase in the heritage area's development. The framework has yielded fruitful results in recent years. At the Summer Palace, for example, professionals restored more than 70 "rooms" — spaces enclosed by four pillars — of the colorful paintings on the beams of its iconic Long Corridor from 2023 to last year. According to Yan Xiaoyu, a senior engineer at the Summer Palace's heritage conservation center, the garden complex was originally built by Emperor Qianlong to celebrate his mother's birthday. Thus, the corridor paintings often feature auspicious patterns, legends from Chinese history and scenes from famous novels. After prolonged exposure outdoors, many of the colors had faded. Before the restoration, researchers studied the original painting techniques, created digital records, and produced replicas for practice. "The restoration result seems good as of now. In this way, visitors can see the beautiful paintings in the Long Corridor more clearly," says Yan. She also mentions the restoration of Suzhou Street in the complex, which is scheduled for completion this year. The street was originally built as a palace shopping street, simulating marketplace transactions when the imperial family toured the area. To give visitors a glimpse of traditional restoration techniques, display windows have been installed on the hoarding surrounding the site during maintenance and closure. The transparent windows allow tourists on the walkway to see what procedures workers are carrying out and what they are repairing. Explanatory boards have also been added. "Located in the middle of the Three Hills and Five Gardens, the Summer Palace is currently the best-preserved garden complex among them. From the history of Chinese garden design, we can see that the complex was essentially the last imperial garden built by a feudal dynasty, so it can be called the crowning masterpiece — a swan song," says Yan. The establishment of the demonstration zone has brought new dynamism to the Summer Palace. Yan says the surrounding environment has been significantly upgraded, with more parks opened to match its historical landscape. "Historically, the Summer Palace was not an isolated garden complex but one closely connected to its surroundings. Now we have restored much of the old landscape so that people can gain a more complete understanding of its historical role," she says. "Upgrading the surrounding environment has also improved the overall ecological environment, so more varieties of birds can be seen in the garden. Now many people go to the west gate to observe birds, making it a new tourist attraction." Beyond protecting old buildings, some garden complexes are also expanding public access to their rich cultural heritage. In 2023, Zhengjue Temple at Yuanmingyuan Ruins Park opened as a museum. In March, the Hanjing Hall at Yuanmingyuan opened to the public after years of archaeological excavations. Qiu Wenzhong, director of the administration of Yuanmingyuan, says that although the site has been backfilled after excavation and people cannot see any buildings above ground, professionals have created transparent display panels featuring line drawings of the original structures. Through the panels, visitors can see the drawings "on" the site and gain a sense of what the buildings looked like during the Qing period. These efforts reflect a broader shift: rather than protecting each site in isolation, the demonstration zone connects individual restoration projects with the wider historical and cultural landscape. "The protection of Three Hills and Five Gardens is in its early stages, but it's never too late. The demonstration zone marks a new beginning. Through joint efforts, we hope to bring more of the landscape's history and cultural richness into view," says Zhu, the scholar.

item.title: NEV brands eye bright export future
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
NEV brands eye bright export future Chinese firms make green transition more affordable and achievable BEIJING — Carlos Alberto Corro Martin used to work for Ebro, an iconic brand of Spain's auto sector that had once faded into memory after its factories fell silent and jobs disappeared. In 2024, with Chinese automaker Chery partnering with Spanish automaker EV Motors, the legendary brand was revived. Electric models rolled off production lines, creating some 1,000 local jobs. "I'm very happy to see it return to the market," said Corro Martin, now a Chery dealer. "I believe the cooperation can open even broader prospects for the Spanish auto industry." Supported by battery technology advantages, intelligent systems and supply-chain efficiency, Chinese new energy vehicle brands are not just winning the hearts of global consumers, but also generating greater spillovers beyond market expansion — creating local jobs, supporting industrialization, and making the green transition more affordable and achievable. In the first eight months, China's total auto exports reached 7.153 million units, up 66.7 percent, including 3.435 million NEVs, a 1.2-fold increase, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Rather than simply shipping cars, many Chinese automakers are building manufacturing and research facilities overseas. In South Africa, Chery inaugurated a manufacturing plant in Rosslyn in July, retaining all 692 employees, with expectations of creating nearly 3,000 jobs across the supply chain. "Chery's investment will pave the way for technology transfer, automation, digitalization and advanced manufacturing systems," said South African Deputy President Paul Mashatile, adding that these developments will strengthen South Africa's industrial capacity. In Brazil, Chinese automaker BYD is embedding research and development, production, sales, services and supply chains into the local economy. Its plant in the state of Bahia employed 5,500 direct workers as of July this year, 86 percent of them from Bahia. Once fully operational, it is expected to support 20,000 direct and indirect jobs, with the company aiming for local suppliers to account for over 50 percent of components by 2027. The expanding footprints of overseas investment come along with the increasing popularity of Chinese NEVs across diverse markets. In Europe, new-car registrations of Chinese brands have for two consecutive months surpassed those of Japanese automakers. In Southeast Asia, consumers in Thailand and Singapore have queued for popular Chinese NEV models, while in the Middle East, Chinese brands have continued to gain traction even amid regional instability. Chinese automakers are also tailoring vehicles to local demands. Chery, now present in over 130 countries and regions, has optimized acceleration and hill-climbing for South America's mountains and strengthened interior sealing for the Middle East's deserts. Chinese NEV brands are especially gaining market share in the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia and other parts of the Global South, according to Ron Zheng, senior partner of Roland Berger and Asia head of automotive practice. "For consumers in these emerging markets, Chinese NEVs are not only affordable, but also offer superior features," Zheng said. In Malaysia, Zeekr, the premium NEV brand under Chinese automaker Geely, entered the market in December 2024. Within months, Zeekr vehicles were more visible on Malaysian roads. "Previously, Malaysians may have associated Chinese cars mainly with affordability," said Zarul Fadzly, sales manager for Zeekr's KLCC and Johor Bahru outlets. "But with the entry of Zeekr and other Chinese brands, they have experienced firsthand the safety, performance and quality of the vehicles. Their perception has changed. Now they are more inclined to pursue the performance and quality of Chinese brands." On the broader impact of Chinese brands entering Malaysia, Fadzly added: "They bring more advanced technology, so other brands will follow suit and compete. Eventually the biggest beneficiaries are consumers — everyone is competing to improve technology." Beyond cost-effectiveness and technological advantages, Chinese NEVs are also accelerating the global energy transition. The International Energy Agency estimated that the global electric vehicle fleet displaced about 1.7 million barrels of oil demand a day in 2025, with China accounting for roughly 1 million barrels a day. Chinese automakers' overseas expansion is currently in its early stages, far from reaching the level of globalization of traditional automotive powerhouses, Zheng from Roland Berger said. item.title: China to further prioritize AI-driven manufacturing
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
China to further prioritize AI-driven manufacturing Efforts urged to make nation's industrial chains more self-supporting, resilient China is putting artificial intelligence at the heart of its next manufacturing push, seeking to make factories smarter and critical supply chains more resilient, while keeping the world's largest manufacturing base plugged into global markets, officials, company executives and industry experts said on Sunday. The message was delivered as the 2026 World Manufacturing Convention opened on Sunday in Hefei, Anhui province. It came just days after China's top leadership called for sustained efforts to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing, and make the country's industrial chains more self-supporting and risk-resilient at a national advanced manufacturing conference in Beijing last week. The timing of the two gatherings underscores a shift in the country's industrial priorities. Xin Guobin, vice-minister of industry and information technology, said at the Anhui convention that China will make a new generation of intelligent manufacturing a priority and push for the deeper integration of AI in manufacturing. "China will cultivate smart factories, develop open-source foundation models and industry-specific AI models, strengthen domestic manufacturing software and hardware, and accelerate the low-carbon transformation of factories," Xin said. That transition is particularly visible in Anhui. Liang Yanshun, Party secretary of Anhui, said that every minute, factories across the province produce about 190 home appliances, 50 laptop computers and four new energy vehicles. "Such momentum benefits from Anhui's decades of technological innovation and intelligent transformation. More and more Anhui-made products are setting sail overseas and benefiting consumers around the world," he said. One of the prime examples is ChangXin Memory Technologies. The Hefei-based memory chip maker said on Sunday that it has begun mass production of its fifth-generation, or G5, DRAM technology platform, which has reached the industry's most advanced manufacturing level. CXMT said that each wafer can now produce over 50 percent more usable memory chips than the previous-generation platform. Its 24GB LPDDR5X mobile memory chips based on the new platform are also in mass production and have been adopted by mainstream Chinese flagship smartphones. LPDDR5X is a type of high-speed, low-power memory chip widely used in premium smartphones, where higher capacity and faster data transfer are increasingly important for AI and other computing-intensive applications. Luo Xiaodong, vice-president of CXMT, said that the company had reduced the half-pitch of the active area in its memory array to 11.95 nanometers, putting CXMT close to the most advanced DRAM manufacturing technologies currently in mass production worldwide. The figure refers to the spacing between key structures inside a memory chip: the smaller the spacing, the more memory cells can be packed onto the same area of silicon. Latest data from the Anhui provincial government showed that during the 14th Five-Year Plan (2021-25) period, revenue from the province's large industrial companies climbed to 5.9 trillion yuan ($866 billion) from 3.8 trillion yuan, taking the province to fifth place nationwide. Carlos Magarinos, global chairman of the Global Alliance of SMEs and a former director-general of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, said that Anhui had made a "profound impression", pointing to the rapid growth of sectors including new energy batteries and electronic information. Industry experts said that for China, the next manufacturing race is no longer simply about making more, but about making smarter and greener, and creating more advanced technology. Tian Jietang, head of the industrial economics department at the Development Research Center of the State Council, said: "China needs stronger advanced manufacturing capabilities and more resilient supply chains to cope with intensifying international competition."

item.title: Paving a win-win path for China and the West
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-21
Paving a win-win path for China and the West Share - WeChat
In a recent interview with China Daily's Global Lens, Alan Macfarlane, professor of social anthropology at the University of Cambridge, noted that the West has had a strong tendency toward binary thinking since ancient Greek times. In his view, this way of thinking profoundly distorts geopolitical and individual relations. "It isn't black and white and simplified. Collaboration and cooperation is good for everyone in facing major problems," he said. Macfarlane added that communication, travel, friendship, and better education of our children could help create a world free from binary opposition.

Turing Award winner: AI for good needs US-China cooperation Share - WeChat
The upcoming US visit by President Xi Jinping serves as a perfect opportunity for launching global AI cooperation led by China and the US, Joseph Sifakis, a Turing Award winner, told China Daily's Global Lens. Instead of letting tech giants dominate the response to transformation brought about by AI, China and the United States — as the two AI superpowers — should take the lead in fostering state-led cooperation, he said. Sifakis also advocated the building of a global AI governance framework, with the participation of Global South countries. Click on the video to watch more.
